text.p: Homegrown hero Saintly looked set on Monday to displace Ireland's Oscar Schindler as favourite for the Melbourne Cup, but government experts forecast victory instead for a long shot from England.
Saintly, whose trainer Bart Cummings has already won a record nine Cups, was quoted at 5-1 by a leading bookmaker to take Australia's premier handicap horse race.
Oscar Schindler, winner of the Irish St Leger and a fast-finishing third in the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe, was still favourite at 4-1 -- but was said to be drifting in the market.
"What we're saying is that Saintly will start as favourite tomorrow, and he'll win the Melbourne Cup," said a spokeswoman for the Darwin All-Sports bookmakers.

Saintly, a four-year-old gelding, won a major Melbourne Cup trial race 10 days ago and trainer Cummings said on Monday he was still improving and should stay the Cup's gruelling 3,200 metres (two miles).
But Oscar Schindler, a giant five-year-old chestnut that has the best race record in the field of 24, was also reported in fine form on training gallops near Melbourne.
Such is the importance of the A$2.2 million ($1.74 million) Cup that race day itself is a public holiday in Australia's second city.

Wider regional rivalries are also put aside for a few minutes and national politicians were told on Monday they too would get 30 minutes off work -- as long as they kept to the point during ministers' question time beforehand.

"There is an event occurring at 3.20 p.m. tomorrow afternoon, namely the Melbourne Cup, for which the whole nation stops and it's only fitting therefore that the parliament joins in the celebration of that great event," Science Minister Peter McGauran told parliament.
While most pre-race punditry has focused on Oscar Schindler, Saintly and last year's winner Doriemus, McGauran threw a new name into the hat -- the English-trained Court of Honour.
He said government mathematicians had factored in the race distance, fitness of the horses, starting draws, weight carried and track conditions to choose the horse.
Court of Honour, trained by Peter Chapple-Hyam, is a 30-1 shot carrying a relatively high riding weight of 56.5 kg.

Like a true politician, however, McGauran hedged his bets, warning MPs that his calculations did not take into account unforeseen factors "such as nobbling, incompetent riding, pot-holes in the track or a monsoonal downpour".
